source.title: Correcting Gradient-Based Circuit Localization via Interaction-Aware Backpropagation
source.authors: Joakim Edin; Casper L. Christensen; Róbert Csordás; T. Ruotsalo; Zheng-Xuan Wu; Maria Maistro; Jing Huang; Lars Maaløe

page_placements.theme: Named sources of compensation other than copy suppression, and how large they are

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. There are minor extraction defects, including missing symbols or references rendered as “??”; the text is not cut off.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports on attention-score self-repair, a related but distinct mechanism. It does not test L10H7’s copy suppression, calibration, or self-repair after ablating an upstream copier, and it does not measure the relative contribution of copy suppression to self-repair.
record.gate_note: The paper’s self-repair experiments concern softmax redistribution among attention positions with similar contributions, not the claimed head’s suppression of a context-present token predicted by earlier components. It cites Copy Suppression but does not test that head or its proposed role. Its own findings about attention-score self-repair are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: This is a gradient-attribution method paper (GIM). It cites Copy Suppression [18] only as a prior source of self-repair via backup heads. It never examines GPT-2 small L10H7, copy suppression, calibration, or the share of self-repair due to copy suppression. Its own 'attention self-repair' is softmax redistribution among redundant positions within one head. That is a different construct from a head suppressing predicted, context-present tokens.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors identify softmax-redistribution attention self-repair, which makes gradients vanish for influential attention scores. They propose GIM, combining TSG, layernorm freeze and gradient norm, and report state-of-the-art MIB circuit localization and strong feature attribution.
record.recipe_differences: The study modifies gradient-based attribution and evaluates attention-score self-repair; it does not perform a circuit-level test of L10H7 copy suppression.
record.method_sensitivity: Self-repair instance counts depend on the model and dataset. Detection uses ϵ = 0.01 and a coefficient-of-variation threshold of 0.1; the paper also reports that changing the latter threshold changes the number of plotted points. TSG performance varies by model-dataset pair and temperature; higher temperatures can degrade performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Within-head attention self-repair is reported: individually ablating either of two high-weight, similar-contribution positions has a smaller effect than ablating both jointly. Instances are counted at 65–1200 per input under the authors' thresholds, across Gemma, LLaMA and Qwen models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Softmax redistribution among redundant attention positions is a distinct source of self-repair that makes single-score ablations and gradients understate importance.

fits_no_version.finding: Temperature-adjusted softmax gradients are described as approximating joint attention-score ablation better than standard gradients. This is method validation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Elevated-temperature softmax gradients better approximate joint attention-score perturbation in self-repair cases.

record.problems: The paper’s self-repair instance detection uses empirically selected thresholds and selects highly ranked attention weights. Most direct comparisons for the cited self-repair examples are figure-only, without reported numerical values or uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No other individual figure-only self-repair comparisons were extracted from Figures 6–13; the text describes additional figures as similar results or threshold variations without providing model-by-model numerical outcomes.

untested.parts: No analysis of GPT-2 small L10H7 or its suppression of predicted, context-present tokens.
No QK/OV circuit analysis of L10H7 and no loss-effect share.
No ablation of upstream copiers, and no measure of copy-suppression compensation.
No test of negative heads in IOI or other models as copy suppressors. IOI on GPT-2 appears only as an MIB benchmark score for circuit localization.
Proposes a new self-repair source (softmax redistribution) but does not quantify it against copy suppression or other sources across the distribution.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only'. The only mention of copy suppression is reference [18], cited as evidence of backup attention heads in the related-work list of self-repair sources. The paper's self-repair notion is within-head redundancy and should not be conflated with V4/V6. Rows r3/r4 are the study's own method comparisons and could be dropped.

versions.untested_parts: No test of GPT-2 small L10H7 or whether it suppresses context-present tokens predicted by earlier components across the training distribution.
No analysis of L10H7’s QK or OV circuits or the claimed 76.9% loss-effect share.
No test of copy suppression’s effect on model calibration or naive copying.
No test of L10H7 copy suppression after ablating an upstream copier.
No test that negative heads in narrow tasks or other models/sizes instantiate the same copy-suppression role.
The paper does not compare copy suppression with other self-repair mechanisms or estimate their relative contributions across the distribution.
